subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - Ecosystems and Biomes Reading
subtitle: Reading practice on biome patterns, food webs, human choices, and case studies.
description: Reading passages and comprehension questions for ecosystems, biomes, food webs, ecosystem services, and human-environment interactions.

data.sourcePassage: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and with nonliving parts of one place. The living parts are called biotic factors and include plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria. The nonliving parts are called abiotic factors and include sunlight, water, temperature, rocks, soil, and air. These parts are connected. If rainfall decreases, plants may grow less. If there are fewer plants, herbivores may have less food. If herbivores decrease, predators may also struggle. A small change in one part of an ecosystem can therefore affect many other parts.

questions.question: Which statement best describes an ecosystem?
options: A community of living and nonliving things interacting in one place
A daily weather forecast for a region
A single country with one political border
A list of all animals in the world
questions.modelAnswer: An ecosystem is a community of living and nonliving things interacting in one place.

questions.question: Which option is an abiotic factor?
questions.modelAnswer: Sunlight is an abiotic factor because it is nonliving.

questions.question: Explain why a decrease in rainfall can affect predators.
questions.modelAnswer: Less rainfall can reduce plant growth. Herbivores then have less food, so their numbers may fall. Predators that rely on herbivores may then struggle to find enough prey.

questions.question: What does this passage suggest about the way ecosystems should be studied?
questions.modelAnswer: Ecosystems should be studied as connected systems because living and nonliving parts affect one another. Looking at only one species or factor can miss important relationships.

data.sourcePassage: A biome is a large region with a similar climate, plants, and animals. Biomes are not spread randomly across Earth. Climate is one of the strongest controls. Near the Equator, strong sunlight and high rainfall can support tropical rainforest. If rainfall is seasonal, savanna may form instead. Around 30 degrees north and south, sinking air makes cloud formation difficult, so many major deserts are found there. Farther from the Equator, temperatures are usually cooler. Near the poles, short growing seasons and cold conditions can support tundra and polar ice. Elevation also changes biome patterns because mountains can be cold even in tropical regions.

questions.question: Which biome is often found near the Equator when rainfall is high?
questions.modelAnswer: Tropical rainforest is often found near the Equator where rainfall is high.

questions.question: Why are many deserts found near 30 degrees north and south?
options: Sinking air makes cloud formation difficult
All rivers disappear at those latitudes
There are no mountains in those areas
questions.modelAnswer: Many deserts form near 30 degrees north and south because sinking air makes clouds and rainfall less likely.

questions.question: How can elevation change the biome pattern shown by latitude?
questions.modelAnswer: Elevation can make places colder than nearby lowlands. A high mountain in a tropical region may have cooler ecosystems than the surrounding area.

questions.question: Why is a world biome map useful even though biome borders are not perfectly sharp?
questions.modelAnswer: A biome map is useful because it shows broad global patterns, such as rainforest near the Equator and tundra near the poles, even though real transition zones are gradual.

data.sourcePassage: People depend on ecosystems for food, fresh water, wood, medicines, fertile soil, flood protection, recreation, and cultural connections. These benefits are called ecosystem services. Some services provide resources directly, such as food or timber. Others regulate natural systems, such as flood control, carbon storage, air cleaning, water filtering, and pollination. Ecosystems also support life by forming soil, cycling nutrients, providing habitat, and allowing photosynthesis. Human activities can damage ecosystems through farming, road building, mining, logging, fishing, pollution, tourism, and climate change. However, people can also protect ecosystems through conservation, restoration, careful planning, and sustainable resource use.

questions.question: What are ecosystem services?
options: Only the animals in a rainforest
questions.modelAnswer: Ecosystem services are benefits people receive from nature.

questions.question: Which example is a regulating ecosystem service?
options: Fresh water taken from a river
questions.modelAnswer: Water filtering by a wetland is a regulating ecosystem service.

questions.question: Explain how people can both harm and protect ecosystems.
questions.modelAnswer: People can harm ecosystems through logging, pollution, mining, overfishing, road building, and climate change. They can protect ecosystems through conservation, restoration, careful planning, and sustainable resource use.

questions.question: Why should decision-makers consider ecosystem services before building on a wetland?
questions.modelAnswer: They should consider ecosystem services because wetlands can filter water, store floodwater, and provide habitat. Building there might reduce those benefits and increase risks for people and wildlife.

data.sourcePassage: The Amazon rainforest is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth. It stores carbon, helps move moisture through the atmosphere, supports many species, and provides resources and livelihoods. Main pressures include cattle ranching, soy farming, logging, mining, road construction, and land-clearing fires. The Serengeti savanna in East Africa supports grazing animals such as wildebeest, zebras, and gazelles, along with predators such as lions and cheetahs. Seasonal rainfall helps drive the Great Migration. The Great Plains in North America are temperate grasslands with fertile soils that support wheat, corn, cattle, and wind energy. The Arctic tundra has permafrost, short growing seasons, and fragile ecosystems affected by warming and development. Coral reefs are warm, shallow marine ecosystems that support biodiversity, fishing, tourism, and coastal protection.

questions.question: Which case study is described as the largest tropical rainforest on Earth?
questions.modelAnswer: The Amazon rainforest is described as the largest tropical rainforest on Earth.

questions.question: Which case study is linked to permafrost?
questions.modelAnswer: The Arctic tundra is linked to permafrost.

questions.question: How does seasonal rainfall help explain the Great Migration in the Serengeti?
questions.modelAnswer: Seasonal rainfall affects where fresh grass and water are available. Grazing animals move across the savanna to find these resources, and predators depend on those prey movements.

questions.question: Choose two case studies from the passage and compare one human pressure or benefit in each.
questions.modelAnswer: The Amazon faces pressures from logging, roads, farming, and mining, but it also stores carbon and supports livelihoods. Coral reefs support tourism and fishing, but they face pressures from warming, pollution, and coastal development.
